---
title: "Transportation Choices"
subtitle: "Share of population within 1/4 mile of a bike or transit facility, by scenario"
date: today
---

## Purpose

How much of the Wasatch Front's population lives somewhere they can actually
*choose* to bike or take transit instead of drive? Transportation Choices
answers that with one number per place: the percent of people within 1/4
mile of a dedicated bike facility, or of a frequent bus route, transit stop,
or station.

That number only means something next to a point of comparison, so we
compute it for three scenarios. Each scenario is a combination of two
independent inputs that do **not** have to match: a socioeconomic (SE)
forecast year, and a GIS facility *vintage* year (what's actually built on
the ground, or assumed built, as of some year).

| Scenario | SE year | GIS vintage | Reads as |
|---|---|---|---|
| Existing 2027 | 2027 | 2027 | today |
| No Build 2055 | 2055 | 2032 | 2055's population, with no further facilities built |
| RTP (Build) 2055 | 2055 | 2055 | 2055's population, with the RTP's planned facilities built |

Comparing No Build against RTP isolates the effect of *building the plan* --
same future population, different infrastructure. Comparing Existing against
either 2055 scenario shows how much of that effect is just growth.

::: {.callout-important}
## The 2032 GIS vintage is a placeholder, not real data

Neither mode has a real 2032 facility layer yet -- bike is waiting on a
layer from Sarah/Hugh (via Suzie), transit on a LIN Stops file from Suzie.
Until those arrive, 2032 is deliberately defined as "unchanged from 2027"
(see `GIS_VINTAGES` below), so **No Build 2055 currently only isolates the
effect of population growth, not a true no-further-investment scenario.**
Re-run this page once the real 2032 data lands.
:::

GIS facility data is *incremental* by vintage year and mode: each vintage
layers new facilities on top of the previous one rather than restating
everything from scratch. That's what makes the pipeline easy to extend --
adding a scenario is one line in `SCENARIOS`, and adding a GIS vintage is one
entry in `GIS_VINTAGES`.

This replaces the `_archive/` v9 arcpy scripts (01-08), which bundled SE and
facility data together per scenario (so SE year and GIS vintage couldn't
vary independently) and filtered transit stops with a hardcoded route list.

## Data Sources

| Mode | Vintage | What's added | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bike | 2027 (base) | On-street bike facilities + trails | `utah_bikeways`, filtered to `Facility1 <> 'Not Available'` |
| Bike | 2032 | *(placeholder -- not yet available)* | TBD, Sarah/Hugh via Suzie |
| Bike | 2055 | RTP 2027 Preferred Scenario AT projects | `at_line_projects`, `at_point_projects` |
| Transit | 2027 (base) | Fixed-guideway stations + frequent bus stops | `uta_stops` + `uta_routes` |
| Transit | 2032 | *(placeholder -- unchanged from 2027)* | LIN Stops, not yet received from Suzie |
| Transit | 2055 | RTP 2027 Preferred Scenario transit projects | `transit_line_projects`, `transit_point_projects` |

Socioeconomic data is WFRC's v10 forecast, one CSV per year (2023-2065) under
`_data/raw/SE_v10_20260921/`. TAZ geometry comes from the `WasatchFrontTAZ`
REST service (`wftcm_taz`).

## Setup

Two dictionaries carry all of the above as data rather than as logic:
`GIS_VINTAGES` encodes what each vintage adds and which earlier vintage it
builds on, and `SCENARIOS` just points at a `(se_year, gis_year)` pair for
each named scenario. Nothing downstream needs to change to add a scenario or
a vintage -- only these two structures do.

```{python}
#| label: setup

from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
from gis_adhoc_analyses.layer_cache import ensure_layers

PATHS = {
    "se_dir": Path("_data/raw/SE_v10_20260921"),
    "output": Path("output"),
}

CRS = "EPSG:26912"  # UTM 12N, meters -- project everything to this before buffering/intersecting

CONSTANTS = {
    "buffer_m": 0.25 * 1609.34,  # 0.25 mi in meters
    "wfrc_county_fips": [3, 11, 35, 57],  # Box Elder, Davis, Salt Lake, Weber
    "se_join_field": "TAZID",
}

# Incremental by vintage year: "adds" are layer keys new at that vintage,
# "builds_on" is the vintage it layers on top of (None = base vintage).
GIS_VINTAGES = {
    "bike": {
        2027: {"adds": ["utah_bikeways"], "builds_on": None},
        2032: {"adds": [], "builds_on": 2027},  # placeholder: layer TBD (Sarah/Hugh via Suzie)
        2055: {"adds": ["at_line_projects", "at_point_projects"], "builds_on": 2032},
    },
    "transit": {
        2027: {"adds": ["uta_stops", "uta_routes"], "builds_on": None},
        2032: {"adds": [], "builds_on": 2027},  # placeholder: treat as unchanged from 2027
        # until LIN Stops (Suzie) arrives -- a deliberate interim choice, not a gap
        2055: {"adds": ["transit_line_projects", "transit_point_projects"], "builds_on": 2032},
    },
}

SCENARIOS = [
    {"name": "existing_2027", "se_year": 2027, "gis_year": 2027},
    {"name": "no_build_2055", "se_year": 2055, "gis_year": 2032},
    {"name": "rtp_2055", "se_year": 2055, "gis_year": 2055},
]
```

## Data Acquisition

Every REST layer any vintage needs gets fetched once, up front, by reading
the keys straight out of `GIS_VINTAGES` -- add a layer to a vintage and it's
automatically requested here too.

```{python}
#| label: fetch-rest-layers

rest_keys = sorted(
    {"wftcm_taz"}
    | {layer for mode in GIS_VINTAGES.values() for v in mode.values() for layer in v["adds"]}
)
L = ensure_layers(rest_keys)
print(f"Fetched {len(L)} REST layers: {rest_keys}")
```

```{python}
#| label: check-se-years

se_years_available = sorted(int(p.stem.removeprefix("SE_")) for p in PATHS["se_dir"].glob("SE_*.csv"))
assert se_years_available, f"No SE files found under {PATHS['se_dir']}"
for scenario in SCENARIOS:
    assert scenario["se_year"] in se_years_available, (
        f"Scenario {scenario['name']!r} needs SE_{scenario['se_year']}.csv -- not found"
    )
print(f"SE years available: {se_years_available[0]}-{se_years_available[-1]} ({len(se_years_available)} files)")
print("All scenario SE years present.")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Workshop-area geography is not reported yet

The v9 pipeline summarized results by workshop area as well as region and
county. No v10 boundary source has been identified for that geography level
-- it will be added to `GEOGRAPHY_LEVELS` in @sec-compute once one exists.
:::

## Build Facility Geometry — Bike {#sec-bike-geometry}

Bike facilities are line geometry, buffered directly: `utah_bikeways`'s
`Facility1` field distinguishes facility type, and `"Not Available"` is the
only value that means *no* bike facility, so everything else -- on-street
bike lanes and trails alike -- is existing network. The 2055 vintage adds
the RTP 2027 Preferred Scenario's active-transportation projects as-is.

```{python}
#| label: bike-raw-by-vintage

bike_raw = {
    2027: gpd.read_file(
        L["utah_bikeways"], where="Facility1 IS NOT NULL AND Facility1 <> 'Not Available'"
    ).to_crs(CRS)[["geometry"]],
    2032: gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[], crs=CRS),  # placeholder: 2032 bike layer TBD
    2055: gpd.GeoDataFrame(
        pd.concat(
            [
                gpd.read_file(L["at_line_projects"]).to_crs(CRS)[["geometry"]],
                gpd.read_file(L["at_point_projects"]).to_crs(CRS)[["geometry"]],
            ],
            ignore_index=True,
        ),
        geometry="geometry",
        crs=CRS,
    ),
}
for year, gdf in bike_raw.items():
    print(f"Bike {year} adds: {len(gdf)} features")
```

Each vintage's cumulative network is its own `adds` plus everything the
vintage it `builds_on` already had -- so a vintage with nothing new yet
(2032, for now) is simply identical to the vintage beneath it, not empty.
Buffering and dissolving that cumulative network once per vintage gives the
geometry every scenario needing that vintage can reuse.

```{python}
#| label: bike-buffers-by-vintage

bike_cum = {}
for year in sorted(GIS_VINTAGES["bike"]):
    builds_on = GIS_VINTAGES["bike"][year]["builds_on"]
    parts = [bike_raw[year]] if builds_on is None else [bike_cum[builds_on], bike_raw[year]]
    bike_cum[year] = gpd.GeoDataFrame(pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True), geometry="geometry", crs=CRS)

bike_buffers = {
    year: gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[cum.buffer(CONSTANTS["buffer_m"]).union_all()], crs=CRS)
    for year, cum in bike_cum.items()
}
for year, cum in bike_cum.items():
    print(f"Bike {year} cumulative: {len(cum)} features")
```

## Build Facility Geometry — Transit {#sec-transit-geometry}

Transit works differently in a way that matters for the buffer, not just the
source: it's built from **stop/station points**, never from route
linework, and only from a *subset* of stops --

1. LRT/CRT fixed-guideway stations, caught by `mode` containing `TRAX` or
   `FrontRunner`, and
2. **frequent bus stops only** -- `uta_routes` filtered to the
   frequent/fixed-guideway service tiers, matched back to stops through the
   comma-separated `route` field.

Every other bus stop is excluded. This two-part filter replaces v9's
hardcoded route list with something that updates itself as UTA's service
changes.

```{python}
#| label: transit-2027-base

_HF_ROUTETYPES_SQL = "'Frequent','BRT','Blue Line','Red Line','Green Line','S Line','FrontRunner'"
hf_route_abbrs = set(
    gpd.read_file(L["uta_routes"], where=f"routetype IN ({_HF_ROUTETYPES_SQL})")["lineabbr"].astype(str)
)

stops_raw = gpd.read_file(L["uta_stops"]).to_crs(CRS)
fixed_guideway = stops_raw[stops_raw["mode"].str.contains("TRAX|FrontRunner|BRT", na=False)]
hf_routes = stops_raw[
    stops_raw["route"].apply(
        lambda r: False if pd.isna(r) else bool({t.strip() for t in str(r).split(",")} & hf_route_abbrs)
    )
]
transit_2027 = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    pd.concat([fixed_guideway[["geometry"]], hf_routes[["geometry"]]], ignore_index=True).drop_duplicates(),
    geometry="geometry",
    crs=CRS,
)
print(f"Fixed-guideway / BRT stops: {len(fixed_guideway)}")
print(f"Frequent-route stops:      {len(hf_routes)}")
print(f"Transit 2027 base (dedup): {len(transit_2027)}")
```

The 2055 vintage adds the RTP's transit projects, but a planned rail or BRT
corridor arrives as a line, not a point -- so each line project is reduced
to its centroid here, keeping the whole transit buffer point-based rather
than letting new corridors buffer like a continuous bike facility would.

```{python}
#| label: transit-raw-by-vintage

transit_2055_lines = gpd.read_file(L["transit_line_projects"]).to_crs(CRS)
transit_2055_points = gpd.read_file(L["transit_point_projects"]).to_crs(CRS)
transit_raw = {
    2027: transit_2027,
    2032: gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[], crs=CRS),  # placeholder: LIN Stops file from Suzie
    2055: gpd.GeoDataFrame(
        pd.concat(
            [
                transit_2055_points[["geometry"]],
                gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=transit_2055_lines.centroid, crs=CRS),
            ],
            ignore_index=True,
        ),
        geometry="geometry",
        crs=CRS,
    ),
}
for year, gdf in transit_raw.items():
    print(f"Transit {year} adds: {len(gdf)} features")
```

```{python}
#| label: transit-buffers-by-vintage

transit_cum = {}
for year in sorted(GIS_VINTAGES["transit"]):
    builds_on = GIS_VINTAGES["transit"][year]["builds_on"]
    parts = [transit_raw[year]] if builds_on is None else [transit_cum[builds_on], transit_raw[year]]
    transit_cum[year] = gpd.GeoDataFrame(pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True), geometry="geometry", crs=CRS)

transit_buffers = {
    year: gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[cum.buffer(CONSTANTS["buffer_m"]).union_all()], crs=CRS)
    for year, cum in transit_cum.items()
}
for year, cum in transit_cum.items():
    print(f"Transit {year} cumulative: {len(cum)} features")
```

## Prepare TAZ Geography

TAZ geometry itself doesn't change across scenarios -- only the population
joined onto it does (that happens in @sec-compute, per scenario). So this
runs once: filter to the four WFRC counties, and add the fields every
downstream calculation needs -- `Region` (a constant, for the region-level
rollup), `CountyName`, and each TAZ's total area in acres.

```{python}
#| label: prepare-taz

taz_raw = gpd.read_file(L["wftcm_taz"]).to_crs(CRS)
print(f"TAZ columns: {list(taz_raw.columns)}")

taz = taz_raw[taz_raw["CO_FIPS"].isin(CONSTANTS["wfrc_county_fips"])].copy()
taz["Region"] = "WFRC"
taz["CountyName"] = taz["CO_NAME"].str.title()
taz["AcresTotal"] = taz.geometry.area / 4046.8564224
print(f"TAZ after county filter: {len(taz)} (from {len(taz_raw)})")
```

## Compute Compatible-Area % by Scenario {#sec-compute}

We don't know how population is distributed *within* a TAZ, only its total
-- so where a facility buffer only partly covers a TAZ, we assume population
spreads evenly across the TAZ's area and credit that TAZ with the same
share of its population: `HHPOPPiece = HHPOP * (piece area / total area)`.
Summing `HHPOPPiece` over all pieces and dividing by total `HHPOP` for a
geography gives the percent of its population within 1/4 mile of a
facility -- which is exactly `SCENARIOS × modes × geography levels` worth of
one number each, so the result is a single tidy table rather than the nine
separate CSVs the old per-scenario scripts produced.

```{python}
#| label: compute-tidy-results

GEOGRAPHY_LEVELS = ["Region", "CountyName"]  # add "SmallArea" once a workshop-area boundary exists

results = []
for scenario in SCENARIOS:
    se_path = PATHS["se_dir"] / f"SE_{scenario['se_year']}.csv"
    assert se_path.is_file(), f"Missing SE file: {se_path}"
    se = pd.read_csv(se_path)
    se.columns = se.columns.str.lstrip(";")  # v10 export has a stray leading ';' on the header row

    taz_se = taz.merge(se[[CONSTANTS["se_join_field"], "HHPOP"]], on=CONSTANTS["se_join_field"], how="left")

    for mode, buffers in (("bike", bike_buffers), ("transit", transit_buffers)):
        pieces = gpd.overlay(taz_se, buffers[scenario["gis_year"]], how="intersection")
        pieces["AcresPiece"] = pieces.geometry.area / 4046.8564224
        pieces["HHPOPPiece"] = pieces["HHPOP"] * pieces["AcresPiece"] / pieces["AcresTotal"]

        for level in GEOGRAPHY_LEVELS:
            totals = taz_se.groupby(level)["HHPOP"].sum()
            piece_totals = pieces.groupby(level)["HHPOPPiece"].sum().reindex(totals.index, fill_value=0)
            pct = piece_totals / totals
            for geography_name, value in pct.items():
                results.append(
                    {
                        "scenario": scenario["name"],
                        "mode": mode,
                        "se_year": scenario["se_year"],
                        "gis_year": scenario["gis_year"],
                        "geography_level": level,
                        "geography_name": geography_name,
                        "pct_near_facility": value,
                    }
                )

tidy = pd.DataFrame(results)
print(f"Tidy results: {len(tidy)} rows")
assert tidy["pct_near_facility"].between(0, 1).all(), "Percentage outside [0, 1] -- check overlay/weighting"
tidy.head()
```

## Outputs

One CSV per scenario, each long-format across modes and geography levels --
easier for a planner to open and filter than nine narrow files, and named so
each scenario's file is unambiguous on its own.

```{python}
#| label: write-outputs

PATHS["output"].mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for scenario in SCENARIOS:
    out_path = PATHS["output"] / f"transportation_choices_{scenario['name']}.csv"
    tidy[tidy["scenario"] == scenario["name"]].to_csv(out_path, index=False)
    print(f"Saved -> {out_path}")
```

## Visualization

@fig-region-pct compares all three scenarios at the region level. Reading
left to right: the gap between Existing 2027 and No Build 2055 is pure
population growth outpacing a frozen network; the gap between No Build 2055
and RTP 2055 is what building the plan actually buys.

```{python}
#| label: fig-region-pct
#| fig-cap: "Share of WFRC-region population within 1/4 mile of a bike or transit facility, by scenario."
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart comparing bike and transit percentages across three scenarios: Existing 2027, No Build 2055, and RTP 2055. Bike rises from about 88% to about 94%; transit rises only slightly from Existing to No Build before reaching about 21% under RTP 2055."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

region = tidy[tidy["geography_level"] == "Region"].copy()
scenario_order = [s["name"] for s in SCENARIOS]
region["scenario"] = pd.Categorical(region["scenario"], categories=scenario_order, ordered=True)
region = region.sort_values("scenario")

MODE_COLORS = {"bike": "#1B7F79", "transit": "#8A5BC2"}  # fixed categorical order, not cycled

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
width = 0.35
x = range(len(scenario_order))
for i, mode in enumerate(("bike", "transit")):
    vals = region[region["mode"] == mode].set_index("scenario")["pct_near_facility"].reindex(scenario_order)
    offset = (i - 0.5) * width
    ax.bar([xi + offset for xi in x], vals * 100, width=width, label=mode, color=MODE_COLORS[mode])

ax.set_xticks(list(x))
ax.set_xticklabels(scenario_order)
ax.set_ylabel("% of population within 1/4 mile")
ax.legend(title="Mode", frameon=False)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(PATHS["output"] / "region_pct.png", facecolor=fig.get_facecolor(), dpi=150)
plt.show()
```
